title: Prosecutors Subpoena Big Banks—Including JP Morgan—For Alleged ‘Debanking,’ Report Says - Forbes
content: Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, is investigating several major banks for allegedly “debanking” customers for political reasons, the Wall Street Journal reported—following up on one of President Donald Trump’s major complaints after his 2020 election loss. Investigators have reportedly sent subpoenas to several major banks, including Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase—one of the banks Trump is suing for closing his accounts following the Jan. 6 Capitol riots. Trump previously signed an executive order last August instructing regulators to examine if banks violated the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the Treasury Department’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is conducting a probe of the allegations. However, sources told the Journal that Pirro’s office was conducting its own probe and did not receive a referral from the Treasury Department office. An official investigation has not been announced as of Wednesday afternoon, and Pirro’s office did not immediately return a request for comment from Forbes. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a preliminary report on the subject in December, finding that nine banks made “inappropriate distinctions among customers” between 2020 and 2023. These included several of the largest banks in the country, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank and Wells Fargo. The preliminary report said the investigation was ongoing, and the office was still reviewing “thousands” of complaints of alleged debanking of individuals based on “political or religious” values. Trump named Pirro, a former prosecutor in Westchester County, New York, and Fox News host, as U.S. attorney for D.C. last May. Since then, her office, as well as the Justice Department at large, has come under fire for pursuing investigations of Trump’s political enemies—including an aborted probe of six Democratic lawmakers who appeared in a video urging members of the military not to follow illegal orders. Her office also launched an investigation of former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell over renovations to the central bank’s Washington, D.C., headquarters. Pirro dropped the probe into Powell in April, but the prosecutor has also suggested she could restart the investigation in the future. Trump has sued two banks for “debanking” him after the Jan. 6 riots—Capital One in March 2025, and JPMorgan Chase in January. In a statement, JPMorgan said the suit had “no merit” and insisted it did not close individuals’ accounts based on “political or religious reasons.” In a February legal filing, JPMorgan acknowledged closing some of Trump’s accounts a month after the Capitol riots. The bank had previously never confirmed if it had closed Trump’s accounts, citing banking privacy laws.

title: JP Morgan Private Bank’s Emily Margolis on how concierge services are evolving for ultra-high-net-worth families - Crain Currency
content: Jasmine Suarez is the editor leading Crain Currency. She is a seasoned financial journalist and editor with a distinguished track record in personal finance, investing and wealth management coverage. She has held senior editorial roles at Fortune, where she led coverage of careers, education and finance; and at Business Insider, overseeing the Personal Finance Insider team. Her work has guided readers through complex financial topics ranging from retirement planning to the evolving landscape of private markets. At Crain Currency, Jasmine brings her editorial leadership and industry knowledge to spotlight the strategic moves of family offices and the broader shifts in private capital. She is passionate about demystifying financial systems and helping readers navigate the intersection of wealth, values and long-term investing. Emily Margolis is the vice president and head of lifestyle services at J.P. Morgan Private Bank’s family office practice, where she works with ultra-high-net-worth clients to connect them with curated providers across travel, healthcare, household management and specialty advisory services. She spoke with Crain Currency about why demand for concierge and lifestyle services is growing, how family offices are deciding what to outsource and what those shifting expectations reveal about the future of family office support. What I'm really seeing is that families are seeking access to services beyond just financial guidance from their wealth manager, whether that's a bank or somewhere else. Through our own research, which includes data on our clients' spending history, interests and conversations with clients around the globe, we've identified six areas that our clients are interested in: luxury travel, outsourced CFO services like bill pay and bookkeeping, private aviation, staffing solutions, art and collectibles advisory and healthcare management. What we try to do is act as a thought partner to our clients—spending time understanding their needs and the intent behind their office and helping them identify and access services that fit their needs so they can reduce friction and inefficiency and get time back. The biggest trend I’m seeing is that clients want more time to focus on what matters most to them. Some families might form a family office for that reason, to address lifestyle and concierge needs, while others may prefer to have their family office focus on strategic priorities like investment management and look to trusted advisors or external platforms to support their broader lifestyle needs. It depends on the category. Planning for luxury travel, for example, can be a major time suck for many ultra-high-net-worth families. I’ve met with many families who have a fully functioning, mature family office, and they don’t want their employees, who are already managing complex schedules, to also be responsible for vacation planning. The value in outsourcing travel is that it gives them access to administrative support and travel experts who can handle the logistics, provide insider access to hotels and experiences and ultimately make the process more efficient. This way, their staff can focus on what they were actually hired to do, like managing investments or other strategic priorities. The same goes for bill pay and bookkeeping. Many clients are seeking aggregated reporting across their portfolios, and we’ve made significant progress in addressing that need through our partnerships. Today, managing bill pay and bookkeeping is considered table stakes for families who want a clear and accurate picture of their balance sheet. Healthcare is a bit more niche. Some clients are focused on longevity and proactive health management, while others simply want help navigating a complex system. One of the common questions we hear in the healthcare space is about health insurance. “Once I sell my business, how do I access private insurance?” or “How do I navigate Medicare?” These topics often come up when clients are retiring early or selling their business. When I first start working with a family, I typically engage in two ways. Sometimes I’m speaking directly with the principal client, and other times I’m working with their family office staff or their executive assistant. When it comes to the principal and their family, I often pick up early signs that things are becoming too complex through our bankers. We become aware of life events or transitions like a move, a business sale or a major family milestone that signal things are in flux and may require additional support. As their adviser, we know when those things are happening, and can help them access third-party resources or solutions. When I’m speaking with family office staff or executive assistants, I often hear that they’ve been tasked with managing areas outside their expertise — like private aviation or complex travel logistics — and aren’t sure where to start. In both cases, our role is to help them navigate these challenges, connect them with resources and make sure they have the support they need as things become more complex. One example that comes to mind involved a family office where the principals had recently started collecting art. The family office staff were highly skilled in areas like investment reporting and trust administration, but they weren’t experts in art management and weren’t sure how to approach tracking, valuing or even buying and selling pieces as the collection grew. During conversations with both the principals and the family office team, it became clear that managing the art collection was becoming too complex to handle in-house. We discussed different options, whether it made sense to hire someone internally with art expertise or to outsource the function. The family ultimately decided to work with one of our partner advisory firms specializing in art and collectibles. This allowed them to access specialized expertise, support proper management and valuation of their collection and gave them the flexibility to scale support as their needs evolved. We've made the decision to actually tackle each of these categories by identifying third-party providers that we've evaluated and with whom we’ve negotiated pricing. This is entirely in response to client demand. I wouldn't describe it as standardizing because it really depends on the category and the client’s needs. For example, I sometimes get very unique requests in the art and collectibles space, and those are never perfectly standard. But it's not ad hoc –– these providers are formally part of our network, so when a client has a need, we’re able to connect them with experienced experts rather than starting from scratch each time. Yes, there are limits to what some ultra-high-net-worth families are comfortable outsourcing, especially when it comes to higher-risk areas like money movement and bill pay. That’s an area where we often see some hesitation or pushback. When we walk through the pros and cons of outsourcing versus keeping services in-house, there are several important considerations. Outsourcing offers advantages like access to advanced technology that you would otherwise have to license, a dedicated team and the ability to mitigate key-man risk if someone leaves. It also means families can leverage a provider’s established risk and control frameworks, rather than having to build those themselves. But some families are extremely private and may not want someone outside their immediate circle to have visibility into their full financial picture, so they prefer to keep certain functions in-house. The trade-off is that they need to plan for continuity if a key team member leaves, and they’re responsible for maintaining their own technology and controls. Having open conversations about these factors and helping families weigh their options is something I spend a lot of time on with clients. Absolutely. A leaner family office is often more likely to outsource, especially when it comes to concierge and lifestyle services. Depending on the intent of the office, they may focus on their investments or CFO-type functions, but when it comes to other lifestyle needs, they often look for a partner or rely on an executive assistant. In many cases, that team benefits from administrative support through a third party. With more mature family offices, these conversations can be especially valuable. They’ll often share how they’ve solved a particular challenge — like whether to hire an in-house art adviser as the principal’s interest in collecting grows — and I can then share those best practices and perspectives with other clients. This exchange of ideas and solutions helps family offices learn from one another and make more informed decisions about when to build expertise in-house and when to leverage external partners. That’s why it’s always helpful to walk through the pros and cons of each approach and highlight the access points that might be missed by not using an external adviser. Interestingly, our family office survey found that larger, more mature offices are twice as likely to view lifestyle and concierge as a priority, which shows that as family offices evolve, most recognize the value of responding to this trend. Absolutely. As the next generation takes on greater responsibility within the family office, they often seek to modernize operations and are more inclined to consider outsourcing a broader range of services. For offices that already have a mature structure and engaged next-generation family members, we find there is genuine interest in discussing these topics — it's a way to engage them. I was just at our next-gen conference in New York, where I spoke a lot about the luxury travel space –– a big investment area for us. We've recently acquired a company that we now use to support our luxury travel offering, and I shared with attendees a range of insights into trending destinations. This was a strong driver for next-gen participants to start conversations with us. There are really two layers. First, travel is highly visible and accessible — whether through social media, pop culture or TV shows — which makes it resonate with younger family members who are following trends, starting to earn their own money and have the freedom to explore on their own terms. For those beginning their professional lives, travel represents both independence and opportunity. Second, for next-gen family members who are starting their own families, travel becomes a way to create shared experiences and lasting memories. We’re seeing a lot of interest in multigenerational trips, where parents, children and even grandparents come together. It’s a way to strengthen family bonds across generations. Beyond travel, we’re also seeing next-gen interest in sports, cultural experiences and a focus on authenticity. Trends in wellness and health optimization are also gaining traction, as younger family members look for experiences that align with their values and lifestyles. We see lifestyle services evolving well beyond traditional concierge, as families look for guidance in navigating everything from yachting and private aviation to holistic risk management and proactive health optimization. Health, wellness and longevity are becoming central themes — families are looking to connect with specialists for advanced diagnostics, genetic testing and personalized health assessments for long-term wellbeing. There’s also growing interest in destination-driven wellness retreats, including medical-grade clinics and programs focused on nutrition, sleep, metabolic health and cognitive performance. For many, this means balancing the demands of supporting aging parents through complex healthcare decisions while also investing in their own health and longevity, especially among the next generation. Looking ahead, we expect this space to move toward full lifestyle management in a truly holistic sense. It’s no longer just about booking a hotel at a trendy spot, but about supporting families across every aspect of their lives — from healthcare optimization and destination-driven wellness retreats to risk management, including cybersecurity, physical security and insurance. These areas are becoming increasingly important as families grow, seek greater privacy and navigate a world shaped by rapid advances in technology and new risks such as cyber threats. We also see the potential for AI to automate many services, like payments and travel bookings, which will drive greater efficiency. But there will always be a need for human expertise, judgment and personal connection. The future will be about striking the right balance between technology-driven execution and the knowledge and care that advisors can provide. Jasmine Suarez is the editor leading Crain Currency. Tesla's stock story can shape how much money and momentum continue to flow into electric vehicles, charging networks, energy storage, and self-driving technology. With Rajat Gupta now covering Tesla instead of longtime bear Ryan Brinkman, J.P. Morgan no longer has an underweight view on the stock. Morgan's price target to $475 from $145, a major reset for a company that has long split Wall Street into opposing camps. The timing also drew notice since J.P. Rather than evaluating Tesla like a conventional car company, Gupta said investors should focus on how the business integrates its products and software. That setup gives Tesla "unique advantages," he said. He also said the market is still not fully accounting for Tesla's potential in self-driving ride services, humanoid robotics, electric vehicles, battery storage, and infrastructure licensing. Compared with Brinkman's more auto-centered view — which put greater weight on Tesla's main vehicle business and on how its valuation compared with other automakers — Gupta's thesis represents a meaningful shift. Tesla's influence stretches beyond its shareholders. A strong Wall Street narrative could help the company invest in batteries, charging infrastructure, software, and energy products that shape the broader EV market. The debate also highlights the risk of tying a company's value to future promises. The bullish case depends heavily on robotaxis, artificial intelligence, and robotics becoming businesses at scale, even as Tesla has faced years of scrutiny over delays and ambitious autonomy claims. Tesla remains one of the biggest players in EVs, but its pricing power, brand strength, and growth story are all under pressure. Investors are watching that tension closely because Tesla still trades at a much richer valuation than traditional automakers do. Whether an EV makes sense for your household depends more on range, charging access, maintenance costs, and insurance than on Wall Street price targets. If you make your next car an EV, you can benefit from the low fuel and maintenance costs that come with ownership, even if Tesla's robotaxi vision remains uncertain. Charging an EV at home is also significantly cheaper than relying on public chargers. Qmerit helps homeowners install Level 2 chargers with free, instant installation estimates. Whether he proves correct will depend on whether the company can turn its biggest ideas into products and services people use. title: Philanthropy is being transformed: New approaches to effective giving - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content: The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Profound change is unfolding across the philanthropy landscape, much of it driven by three converging forces: As a result, the sector has begun to respond to urgent challenges with greater flexibility, collaboration and purpose. Here’s what you need to know right now: The AI starting point for most nonprofits—as well as for donors and foundations—is to use the technology to improve research, streamline operations, handle day-to-day communications tasks and speed grantmaking workflow. Even at this early stage of adoption, we see AI fundamentally changing the way donors give and manage philanthropic activities. Indeed, in a 2025 survey of more than 600 social sector leaders, The Center for Effective Philanthropy (CEP) found 78% of nonprofits and foundations are using AI tools for internal productivity. Organization leaders noted, “AI has been helpful for drafting emails, policies, procedures, meeting summaries and other documents.” Additionally, many foundations are using AI to help simplify the granting process.1 As an example: One family foundation has used its resources to develop a free AI-powered tool for grantmakers that streamlines the financial due diligence process—a typically resource-and time-intensive task. Using AI, the tool analyzes a grant-seeking organization’s financial records, including audited statements, and generates a scorecard and summary based on criteria selected by the grantmaker—e.g., the financial metrics most relevant to their assessment priorities. At the same time, the tool makes it easy for the nonprofit seeking funding to submit financial documents, ultimately benefiting all parties involved. Foundations and nonprofits using AI in day-to-day workflow share a common set of concerns related to security, data accuracy, staff expertise and built-in bias, according to the CEP survey. Specifically, a majority of philanthropy leaders polled were concerned about: While foundations are leveraging AI in their own operations, few have put guardrails in place to ensure stakeholder trust isn’t eroded: A 2024 survey by the Technology Association of Grantmakers (TAG) showed only 30% of foundations have established policies for using AI, and less than 10% have advisory groups addressing both AI technology and policy.2 A further sign of AI mistrust within the sector: Just 10% of U.S. funders accept grant applications containing AI-generated material, according to 2024 research conducted by Candid, a leading source of data on the nonprofit sector.3 Donors, too, have multiple concerns about AI, with the potential for data security and privacy risks at the top of their list. Also worrying them: the potential for misinformation or inaccurate results and uncertainty about the best ways to use AI.4 To counter these concerns, many donors are supporting initiatives that prioritize safe, equitable and ethical AI development. One such effort is being led by Humanity AI. This five-year, $500 million collaborative grantmaking fund was launched in 2025 by a coalition of philanthropic foundations that support the arts, labor and work, democracy, education and personal safety and security amidst AI advancements. This new organization is committed to putting people and the planet at the center of AI development by ensuring communities have a say in AI design, development, deployment and governance. Specifically, it prioritizes creating an economy where AI enhances rather than replaces workers; holds AI builders to high safety standards; and protects human creativity and artists' work from theft.5 As AI continues to advance, its role in philanthropy will only expand. Balancing innovation with oversight will be key to ensuring AI serves the greater good in the philanthropic sector. Increasingly, donors are moving beyond traditional avenues of giving, such as private foundations, to achieve complex social and environmental impact goals. This more holistic approach uses a mix of charitable vehicles to maximize impact, including 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations, limited liability corporations (LLCs), private operating foundations and, most notably, donor-advised funds (DAFs). Each vehicle serves a unique purpose and, when used in tandem, affords donors greater flexibility, and expands the range of causes and organizations they support. For example: A standout among giving vehicles, these charitable giving accounts allow donors to: DAFs have experienced remarkable growth in recent years, with the number of donor accounts reaching 3.59 million and contributions topping $90 billion, the largest annual totals to date, according to updated figures in the DAF Research Collaborative’s Spring 2026 report.6 As a result, DAFs now account for 15.1% of all charitable giving and 22.8% of individual giving, underscoring their rising popularity among donors who want efficient impact with their philanthropy.7 Growing usage of these vehicles by individuals and families is confirmed by recent data from J.P. Morgan’s own DAF program, the J.P. Morgan Charitable Giving Fund (CGF): Donor-advised accounts are also gaining ground with families, particularly as a vehicle to engage younger generations in charitable giving. These funds streamline digital processes facilitate new donors easily identifying and lending support to passion projects and causes. Further, overseeing a smaller DAF account can serve as a succession planning strategy, allowing children and grandchildren to gain hands-on philanthropic experience before they assume leadership roles in a family foundation. This knowledge and stewardship experience will be critical as an estimated $124 trillion will transfer between generations by 2048, with $18 trillion anticipated to go to charity.8 Finally, DAFs effectively facilitate donor partnership through collaborative funds by pooling resources and sharing risk among donors to maximize impact. Such partnerships also create opportunities to learn from peers, broaden perspectives and raise the profile of important issues. All of which can be enticing to both younger and/or less  experienced donors. While traditional multigenerational (i.e., perpetual) private foundations remain a dominant vehicle for philanthropy, a growing number of donors are embracing time-limited philanthropy. This giving while living ethos, which prioritizes deploying charitable capital within a set timeframe, is gaining significant donor interest. Recent examples run the gamut from a mid-size family foundation recently established with the intention to spend out in 10 years, to the very public announcement of the Gates Foundation to sunset in 2045. More anecdotally, time-limited philanthropy has become a frequently queried topic for J.P. Morgan Philanthropy Advisors, as donors evaluate the trade-off of impact during lifetime or future impact. Meanwhile, research by the National Center for Family Philanthropy also reveals growing donor interest in time-limited family foundations: Historically, few entities founded before the 1990s considered a spend-down model. However, in the last five years, the number of U.S. family foundations with pre-determined lifespans has increased from 9% to 13%, and more than 28% of those surveyed are considering such a move.9 This shift to increased giving during one’s lifetime reflects the growing desire among philanthropists to witness firsthand the impact of their giving and to respond swiftly to urgent social and environmental needs. Though, in some cases, interest can also be attributed to donors recognizing that family foundation succession plans are not always viable; for example, if younger generations have different philanthropic interests or prefer to deploy charitable capital in alternative ways. As more families, individuals and boards institute a spend-down model, embrace new tools and technologies, and prioritize impact now over legacy later, the template for successfully stewarding charitable capital will become ever-more nuanced, and innovative. Bill Ackman has kicked off marketing for the initial public offering of his hedge fund and closed-end fund, adopting a dual-listing approach and expecting to raise between $5 billion and $10 billion. The combined IPO will result in two companies being taken public. This includes Pershing Square Inc. In its filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Pershing Square stated that it has already secured $2.8 billion in commitments ahead of the IPO. In a letter to shareholders, the billionaire investor touted “extraordinary economic characteristics” of Pershing Square as he sought to explain the fund’s long-term goal. “Our long-term goal for Pershing Square Inc. is to build one of the most valuable companies in the world by generating one of the best long-term performance records of any investor ever,” Ackman said. He added that, with permanent capital, Pershing Square has the ideal structure to pursue its investment strategy, which involves acquiring and long-term owning what the company considers some of the greatest businesses and long-term compounders of shareholder value. Ackman also explained that PSI can be considered a “meta” company, earning long-term fees from funds invested in high-quality businesses. He said that Pershing Square’s focus on liquid, large-cap stocks allows it to adjust positions easily and stay invested without pressure from investor flows. Investors who subscribe to shares of Pershing Square USA will also receive shares of the hedge fund, Pershing Square Inc. According to the SEC filing, investors who buy 100 shares of the closed-end fund PSUS will also receive 20 shares of the hedge fund, PSI.
